utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we continue, the -- picking up on where we left off yesterday in terms of today's scheduling, against the goal of - and let me say parenthetically that we have just confirmed this through VWS with the witness - against the goal of having the witness released today, we are in the process of investigating the possibility of sitting beyond the time indicated yesterday afternoon, to accommodate Mr. Krgovic's re-examination. And the present disposition of the witness is that it may be -- it may mean that we would take the -- a break at 1.30 and resume at 2.30, but that remains to be seen. That's still in the process of being worked out. Ms. Korner, was there something that you wished to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the first on that, of course, I -- I -- I'd be very grateful if could I have an extra 15 minutes on top of the 20 minutes, given that we started late. I do need every second to finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We're not unmindful of how these investigations have affected you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, no, I just wanted -- yesterday, when -- in -- effectively in response to something the witness said, I, without having had an opportunity to check, paraphrased what I understood he'd said about delegation of powers, and I was invited to go for the -- remind the witness of the actual words he'd used in the transcript, and of course because it'd arose ex improviso, I didn't have it, but I checked it last night and the relevant parts are at pages 23703 -- 23704, and further, in 23805, and effectively at 23704, "The president was the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces," said the witness, "but the president cannot exercise command over the army." So what he was -- I think was being put to him and what he was agreeing with, was that it was the president's powers as Commander-in-Chief of the army that were delegated to or could be delegated to the Chief of Staff or the head of the staff. And then, later, he -- he -- it was -- the question, I think this was Mr. Cvijetic, at page 23085: "The minister of the interior within the ministry may order this kind of use," that's combat activities, "but exclusively by doing so and executing an order of superior command. He can never do it independently," it was put. And the answer was: "Yes." So effectively what's being suggested to the witness or what was being suggested to the witness was that if the minister of the interior wanted to order the use, it had to be on the basis of superior command, which I take to be the president. And that's what the witness says. I'm not saying that's what we accept, but therefore my summary of it was, I agree, inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So the Registry is now requested to make the necessary arrangements to facilitate the extended sitting this afternoon. Thank you. Could we have the witness back on the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the -- I remind you, before Ms. Korner continues, that you're still on your oath. And the -- we have received your communications in terms of the -- how we are going to proceed for -- for the rest of the day, and we still expect that you would be released by the end of today's -- today's sitting. Although that may -- may be a little longer than we had indicated yesterday. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, could we have, please, another look at the document you were asked a great deal about it in -- by Mr. Krgovic, I believe, and also Mr. Cvijetic, and that's the 1st of July Talic order, which is, I think 1D406. Tab 44 in our binder. It was also in the Defence binder. Yes. This is General Talic, on the 1st of July, setting out, as it were, zones of responsibility to try, presumably, to make things more efficient. Were you aware that on the 1st of July, 1992 Operation Corridor was still going on?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. I think that Operation Corridor went on at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go to the particular line that's caused so much controversy, if you like, that's on page 2, I think both in English and B/C/S. Now, it says: "In the conduct of combat activities all police forces shall be placed under the command of the zone commander," he has divided things into zones, as we saw, in the earlier part of this order, "who shall decide how they are used." That would mean, would it not, General, that what he is talking about there is if there are police units which have been resubordinated for the purposes of combat, it is the zone commander who will decide how they're to be used in that combat. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this is a very precise order, and I agree with you that the corps commander specifies under which conditions in the carrying out of combat activities all police forces shall be placed under the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But I think -- it's not -- one shouldn't read it as meaning that every police force within every zone commander is under that command, should one? It should be read as when the police are being used for the purposes of combat, in other words, resubordinated to the army, it's the zone commander who has the ultimate decision as to how they are used?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the question is which forces those are and how strong they are, if that's a what you mean. We would have to be acquainted with the specific situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite. And if one looks at the next page, which is the distribution list, that is all the subordinate commands to the 1st Krajina -- units, sorry, and, as we can see, it doesn't include, does it, any of the CSB chiefs or anything like that, or the minister?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. So I won't ask you about that. Now could we move, please, again to the -- a document you were asked about before, which is the July 11th meeting of the MUP, and that is document number P160. And it's tab 49A. And that was a document that you hadn't seen, I think, until you got here, because it's not on your bibliography. If we look, please, at item 13 of the conclusions of the meeting, which is page 24 in English, and I think it's page - difficult to tell - I think it may be about the same page in B/C/S. Yep. Thank you very much. "In order to overcome the identified problems and issues of jurisdiction between the MUP and the army of the Serbian Republic, we need to prepare a joint meeting an outline all the problems and agree on a solution to assure [sic] more effective co-operation and co-ordinated action." And then they set out the particular issues that we can see. Paramilitaries. And over the next page in English, problems about engagement of police in combat, co-ordinated action of the army and the MUP on crime prevention, and so on and so forth. Would you agree, General, that that suggests that although in your mind, and possibly in the mind of army officers, it was clear who had the authority, this was not entirely clear to the police side of it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is possible that this created huge problems for the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Because although, as you say, the military view was that they had the right to do anything they wanted effectively, that was not a view shared by the police?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I put it that way, that the military could do whatever they wanted. But they had the right to take a police officer who was under work obligation and transfer him to the status of military conscript under the law. And then he becomes a military person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's what you say. And it may well be that in theory you're right. But that's actually not what happened, was it, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, madam. I'm -- I'm saying how it should be in accordance with the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then move then, please, a little further on in time. Can we come, please, on the same topic, though, as this whole question of resubordination. And could we look, please, at another law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now you said, General, in answer to a question -- this is at page 23693 of the transcript, and it's on the third day of your testimony. I think it was -- it was Mr. Krgovic. He said: "General," a question, "when drafting your report, did you come across any rules about the competencies of the command of the land army in the VRS, and I have in mind 1992?" And you said: "I didn't come across such a document." Well, I'd like you to have a look, please, at the provision, entitled: "Provisional Service Regulations," which is document, please, 20248, and it's at tab 66A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I don't know if it was correctly interpreted, but I spoke about the corps role of the land army. That is a specific document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were quoting from a specific document. The rule of the land army of the JNA, and then I moved onto the adequate rule of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry, that's not the way it came out. If the translation was in error, that's one thing. But it followed on from a number of pages of discussion on the schematic, the supreme commander, then the documents that the General had looked at and said he came across certain documents where one finds the president of the republic is authorising the commander of the Main Staff, and so on and so forth. And then the question as recorded at the top of page 2569 -- sorry, 23693: "When drafting your report, did you come across any rules about the competencies of the command of the land army in the VRS?" Now if Mr. Krgovic tells me that that's not what he meant to say or if the translation is wrong, then, of course, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, General, you weren't meant -- by that answer, you weren't intending to say that there were no laws or regulations relating to command and control drafted in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is difficult for me to remember what I said. I think I meant that in order to explain the topic and the problem, the rules and regulations I was able to find in the Republic of Serbia were sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ah ... yes, that may be so, but -- all right. It's not that you're asserting, General, that no rules and regulations were drafted during the course of 1992 that had affected command and control of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not assert that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we, in any event just have a quick look at this document. Although it was entitled provisional service regulations, it said it applied from the day of their adoption --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we need to go, please -- well, first of all, can we have a look at the second page in English and the second page in the B/C/S, the distribution list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This was being sent on, in fact, by Mr. Vukelic from the 1st Krajina Corps. It's their version of it, so we can see it's sent to their units. And, again, we'll see that it's not sent to any police, CSB, to the minister, or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we look at the fourth page in English and B/C/S. Yep. Sorry, no. Fourth page -- oh, fifth page in English then. Sorry. It's the right page in B/C/S but it's the fifth page in English, please. The Presidency of the Serbian Republic adopted in a session held on the 18th of August, 1992, the provisional service regulations of the army. And it's signed and stamped in the original by Karadzic. Can we just look, please -- can we move on, then, another one, two -- another three pages. It's page 8 in English, and in B/C/S -- and B/C/S, it's, yes, yes, three pages as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Headed: "Rights and Duties of Army Members. "2. Persons employed in the army are military personnel and civilian employees. Military personnel are soldiers, cadets, active-duty servicemen, and reservists, while serving in the army. And active-duty services [sic] are commissioned officers, non-commissioned officers, and contract soldiers. Civilian employs are civilians performing certain specialised jobs in the army." There's no mention there, is there, in defining who is a member of the army and police officer who are resubordinated under the powers of Article 104?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in this specific article, and I add that I would have to read the entire document, but in this article you are right in saying that police officers belonging to the army force are not mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, as I say, General, you can a copy of the whole thing. But if I'm wrong, I'm sure I will be corrected by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it doesn't appear this is in the law library unless we've missed it, but -- so it should be added, I believe, and we can probably do that by agreement, unless I hear any objections to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... law library.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, not according to us it isn't. I mean, only if -- but it may well be we've missed it somewhere because the title in English is quite often not what -- not. Now, right, can we move, please, now to have a look at a document which is P611. And it's at tab 74.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is another one of the reports on the state of morale. This is for August 1992. Done by -- in fact, it comes from the General, apparently. If we go to the last page. I think it's signed on his behalf. All right. And now can we go back, please, to the body, and it's paragraph 2, which is on page 3 in English, and page 4, I think, in B/C/S. Yes. I merely want to ask you if you agree that this is an example of co-operation: "The overall political and security situation in August 1992 was characterised by the following: The activities of several paramilitary governments ... armed formations, increased extremism towards Muslim and Croatian population," and so on, "and a continued effort to place the organs of the authorities and the MUP, Ministry of Interior, above the military formations and the army" I ought to know what RiK stands for, but I can't remember, "system." So stopping there, for a moment, General, does that again, is that a demonstration in this report of what appears to be, from the army's point of view, a misunderstanding of who's in charge?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, it's hard for me to confirm that, because, here, I believe, the report is about problems in the field, about the conduct of some authorities and the MUP. And that's how I read it. And as we see, it says the attempt to place themselves above military formations and the system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it goes on to say: "For these reasons the 1st Krajina Corps commander held a meeting with all unit commanders and municipal presidents at which he pointed to the problem of the existence of para governments and paramilitaries and the need to overcome the crisis in view of the objectives of the war we are waging and at --" I think that must be "at the present time." Would you accept from your knowledge of the period, the documents you've looked at, either for the purposes of report or elsewhere, that although there were tensions between the political, the army, and the police, and arguments about jurisdiction, all three shared the same goal?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Korner, it should be understood that all these elements should be aimed at protecting the Serbian people, if I understand your question correctly. As for how they individually interpreted that goal or implemented it on the ground, one can partly see from what is noted here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. And you would say, I accept because you said it before, that the goal was the defence the Serbian people. The report goes on to talk about the tensions in Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor, because of the large number of arrested citizens for whom there is no evidence or criminal reports that they participated in armed rebellion. And then it goes on to talk about the CSB in Prijedor. Just pausing there for a moment, General, you've not been shown any of the documents that come out from the -- from Manjaca camp, have you, by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, Madam Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can we put it this way: They're not in your bibliography, none of them have turned up in the list of documents that the Defence were going to show you, even if they didn't show them all. So if they're not there, can we take it that you weren't shown them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the last thing I want to deal with on this document is -- relates to something we're going to come on to in a moment. Could we have a look, please, at the third paragraph, the effect of military organisation and war operations, and that's two pages on, I believe, in both English and B/C/S. It should be page 7 on the top -- no, next page, sorry, in B/C/S then, sorry. And it's page 6 in English. And the second paragraph begins: "The prevention of these occurrences," he has described what's been going on, "lies in the fact that a state of war has not been declared ..." Now, you said in your mind there was no difference between an imminent threat of war being declared and a state of war. But it appears, and we've seen it in other documents, General, or the Court has, that certainly to the mind of General Talic it would appear there was a difference, do you agree, from this one statement?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Korner, I think that I said that there was no difference. But as for the authority of certain commanders and structures in each of those states, it's difficult for me to give an assessment of this report of the corps commander from the position that I am in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But can I put it this way: Wasn't the difference, as far as the military were concerned, that in a state of war their powers to take command and control were increased, which did not happen when it was simply an imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Korner, my opinion is that, regarding the authority of the commanders, there is no major difference between the immediate threat of war and the state of war, but there is a difference in the procedures, deadlines, and similar based on my knowledge of these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The final sentence of this paragraph is, I suppose we should go on. He is talking about "... bad interpersonal relations under -- undermined by alcoholism, lack of principles, failure to take measures to protect troop lives. The most prominent example in the negative sense is Colonel Lisica, who, despite personal courage, also demonstrates personal arrogance." Now can we move from that document, please, to document which is P683. It's the next tab, 74A. And this goes back to what we were talking about, about the use of police and leaving the police undermanned. This is to the CSB, written on behalf of Simo Drljaca, chief of the SJB, Prijedor. On 15th of September 1992 the Prijedor SJB received a telephone call from Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic from the Prijedor garrison who said "a telex had arrived in the garrison from the 1st Corps signed by the commander, General Talic requesting --" Now, can we just make sure that's the word, "requesting"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... that 100 policemen from the reserve police force of Prijedor SJB be put at the disposal of the Army of the Serbian republic ... by 1400 hours." "We are unable to meet the request of the 1st Krajina Corps because we do not have this number," of this policeman whom we can set aside, and he explains why. "Earlier this month, we took 417 policemen including seven active police policemen off the roster and gave them to the Serbian army in order to go to the Han Pijesak area. "If we were obliged to meet the request of the 1st Krajina Corps, we would be forced to give up policemen from the Prijedor reserve force." So, General, doesn't it appear that despite your assertions of what the law and the regulations say, it was not an order from the army, it was a request, which Drljaca said he couldn't meet, and he had reported it up to his chief of the CSB, Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Madam Korner. In several places here, the word "request" is mentioned and not "order" or "command."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And doesn't this also square with what I was putting to you yesterday that were policemen were to be used by the army it had to go up through each side's chain of command. Here we see General Talic sending an order to the lieutenant-colonel, who, at his level, puts in the request to the SJB, and the SJB chief says, Sorry, no can do, and reports to his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Korner, I agree that it would have been better had the mutual communication been better and if this were to be resolved jointly. But I think that we could clarify that there are situations in law when the commanders can decide on their own, as I said, to transfer a policeman from the work duty to the military service duty. And perhaps that clarification of mine would help to clear up any dilemmas that you might have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. You're saying, your reading the rules and regs as they applied in the JNA, and prior to this war, mean that's what can happen. But that is clearly, I would suggest, not what either the army or the police thought, is it? Not in 1992 in the VRS. Or maybe -- I'm sorry. It's not what the police thought, I suggest, and I suggest it was unclear to the army as well.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, Madam Korner, that people in war time did not study the regulations well or were not familiar with them in the proper way. On both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then look very quickly at a document I think you already looked at. It's the second communication from Zupljanin about this question of the relationship between the army and the police. It is document P1094, tab 75.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Zupljanin in this is, the 18th of September, is making his position absolutely clear not only to the SJBs but he is copying it to the minister for information, to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, and to the leaders of the organisational units in the CSB. "In recent times there has been an increasing number of requests ..." Can I confirm with you that the word is "requests"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... from lower commands of the army of the Republika Srpska on the territory of Banja Luka ... for the engagement of active and reserve forces of the police in army formations on lines of contact with enemy forces ... requests for the departure of police ... to protect corridors ..." "With regard to the above, I draw the attention of the security of the SJB chiefs to the following: In accordance with the agreement of the most senior representatives of the army and the Ministry of Interior, the Banja Luka CSB ordered the adjustment of the reserve police force to bring it down to the lowest possible ratio ..." Now, is the thinking behind that that if you reduce the number of reserve police, then you increase the number of men who are available to serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in every municipality or republic or region, there is an authorised organ dealing with the defence matters, and they have records of all the military conscripts. In the event of mobilisation and the imminent threat of war, these people, based on their earlier war time assignment, would report to the place where their war time assignment was so that, here, the chiefs of the public security services and unit commanders could, depending on the situation, reduce or increase the numbers or ask that authorised organ to assign these people, pursuant to their assignment and organisation, according to establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, my question is a simple one, and I'm not quite clear that you're answering it. You're either a reserve police officer or you're a reserve military officer, correct, after you've done your military service?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not quite like that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, maybe I better give you the -- but is the idea --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all I want to know is, if -- if you agree with this, and if you don't, then say so and I'll move on because it's not the point I want to deal with. That if you decrease the number of reserve police, you thereby increase the pool of those available to serve in the military.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer affirmatively, Madam Korner, because, besides the military duty, there is the material obligation and the obligation to serve in the civilian protection, so that does not necessarily mean that these people would end up in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, okay. I think we can agree on this, just to move on, that decreasing the reserve police pool enables those persons who are no longer reserve policemen to be assigned to other war time tasks?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, at the bottom of the page in English: "At the same time, we draw to the attention of SJB chiefs the fact that members of the active and reserve police forces may be engaged in combat activities according to the principle of resubordination to a superior army command only in the event that combat activities are taking place on the territory covered by the designated SJBs and with the approval of the chief of the SJB [sic]." So do you understand that to mean, and I hope it's the same in the Serbian language, it's been translated, that Zupljanin is saying here that, As far as I, the chief, am concerned, you cannot, as an SJB chief, allow your officers to be resubordinated unless the combat activity is taking place within your territory, and I, Stojan Zupljanin, have approved?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how I can comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rather would not comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you wouldn't, General, because it doesn't square with what you have been propounding. But this document is not just what Stojan Zupljanin thought about it, and I agree only he could tell us, but he meant it to be read, as he says, in the next page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we turn over -- sorry. Can we turn over. Can we go to the next page in English and also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may not be able to see that, what I just read to you, because it was on the next page. Do you see the part I've just read to you? And I'm sorry, General, I didn't realise that we hadn't -- you hadn't got it. And then it says: "In order to achieve full collaboration and synchronisation of the work of the army and police of Republika Srpska, I ask corps commanders to draw this to the attention of their subordinate commands, through their lines, and brief them on the agreements that were established at a high level." It cannot be read any other way, can it, General, other than the way I suggested?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think here Mr. Zupljanin, and it says here: "I kindly ask the corps commander to draw the attention of the lower-ranking commands."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you pause there for a moment. The word "kindly" doesn't appear in the English translation. Where do you say that appears?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I interrupted you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I quote the last paragraph: "In order to achieve collaboration and synchronisation of the work of the army and police of Republika Srpska, I ask corps commanders to draw this to the attention of their subordinate commands through their lines and brief them on the agreements that were established at joint meetings at the highest level."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And you -- and from -- you deduce what from that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Korner, I told you how I interpret the rules and regulations. I can see that the practice was different, and I emphasise that, in exceptional circumstances, the commanders could take people on their own from work duty and transfer them to the military duty. And in other cases, the regulations intend for this to be done by the authorised organ upon the request of the units, military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I think you've dealt with that. All right. Can we now move, please, to another aspect of matters you were asked about. You were asked -- just get this right. Yes. This was the -- a question of disciplinary -- who would discipline them. And you were shown the document from General Talic about deserting Prijedor policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we look, please -- no, I'm sorry. That's -- it is a topic I want to deal with, but it's not the one. I want to look at, please, the documentation surrounding the General Lisica, Colonel Lisica, as he was then, and Mr. Bjelosevic, chief of the Doboj CSB correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because you were only shown one letter and I would like you to look at that in context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So could we have a look, please, at the document which is P683 -- no, sorry. P -- sorry, yes. 1D283 -- 263, which is at tab 75A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is Bjelosevic to, in fact, Colonel Lisica, who responds to it. 2nd of October. "Due to the worsening security situation in the area of Serbian municipalities" et cetera, et cetera, "... we are forced to withdraw the police from combat operations on the front in Bosanski Brod and Gradacac..." Do you accept that he's not saying "please, may we withdraw," he's telling Colonel Lisica that he is going to withdraw them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it appears to be, Ms. Korner, but you cannot say definitely whether he is asking him to do that or making the decision to do that. Perhaps he is just informing him of the situation. It's difficult to say what the word "forced to" means and what the consequences of that would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. He goes on to say: "We will carry out the withdrawal of the police from these fronts on the 4th of October, 1992." In the last -- he then complains about uniformed -- he wants closer ties with the military police. "We hope you will correctly understand the reasons why we are forced to withdraw the police from the battle-field. We also expect your positive reply with regards to our request to organise and achieve a higher level of association..." Now, let's look at the only document that you were actually shown at -- and I take it you were not shown the original letter by the Defence because it wasn't on their list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I think Ms. Korner is talking about the Stanisic Defence and is talking about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there linked document. There is a request, this one, and then there is a reply by Commander Lisica to this where he does say, I do not permit that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, I am just about to come to that, and I made it clear I was just about to come to that. But my complaint is that -- or the General has confirmed, rather by my complaint, that a selected number of documents were shown, which I suggest are out of context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can we have at a look at the only document in this series that you were shown by the Defence, which I was just about to, which is tab 90 -- 92 of the Defence binder and is one --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is an inappropriate comment. Ms. Korner is leading the witness wrongly. She said that this document hadn't been shown, which is wrong. It had been shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's ask the General rather than having this unseemly --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, were you shown this document by either Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Cvijetic, the one that we just looked at on the screen, which is the first letter?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I will be as fair as so far. If it was shown to me and if it can be found in my bibliography then I seen it, because I made an oath to speak the truth, but I don't remember every single document. If it was shown to me, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go then, please, to the document that you actually looked at in court. As I say, that is Defence document 1D264.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've got it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the reply you were shown. Oh, no, it isn't. We haven't got it up. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have it up, please. 1D264.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the reply from Colonel Slavko Lisica, saying: "I've understood your --" he calls it a proposal. "We're satisfied with their work. We're going to pull them out for a rest, and the reasons you provided are valid, but you don't understand the situation we are in." It was actually Mr. Cvijetic who was asking you about this because he went on about there was Colonel Lisica putting defence above everything. And then can we look at the last of -- letter in this, please, at -- which is 1D265, which is at tab 75B. Now, did you see this letter, Colonel -- General? I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, my reply would be the same in respect of all documents. If it was shown to me, and if it's in my bibliography then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, well it's clear it's not in your bibliography and you weren't shown it in the court. 6th of October, Mr. Bjelosevic writes back saying: "I received your reply of the 3rd --" and there's an order which he's talking about, the 4th, which I don't believe we have. But anyhow. "... all the more since I believe the co-operation between TG 3 and Doboj CSB has been excellent. Did we not fulfil each and every one of your requests, put at your disposal a vehicle," and so on. Whilst I was issuing -- could you -- the English here is rather odd. Could you just read the sentence that comes after the words "poorly equipped"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I quote: "While I was giving approval for the engagement of the police in combat, without my consent or an order of the minister of the interior, there was looting and disorder at a massive scale behind the lines, and particularly, by military deserters ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. If you stop there, thank you, because that's the only part I want. All right. So reading that, if we look at this, the overall picture is Bjelosevic writes to Lisica saying, I'm pulling the troops out. Lisica says, No, you can't. And Bjelosevic then writes back complaining that they co-operated and that approval has been given by him for the use of police in combat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, that's what one can conclude judging on this correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And if, as is -- as General Talic complained, Colonel Lisica is a very arrogant officer, then the -- I suppose can we put it this way, it's a matter of common sense, isn't it, that the relationship between the police and the army, at the lower levels certainly, and possibly at higher levels, would -- might depend on the character of the persons involved?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, Ms. Korner, but I'm saying here how people should act and what is in line with the rules and regulations. I would like to reiterate that the commander has the right to take police officers who are under work obligation and change their status to become military conscripts. What you asked me yesterday - and I'm trying to help you here and provide a foundation - who instigates proceedings, that depends on the status of the police officer at that point in time; whether they are under work obligation or military conscripts. And I can add that this is provided for by the Law on All People's Defence from 1982. That's a document which I enclosed, and in Articles 23, 24, 25, and especially 26, that -- or, rather, all that regulates work obligation. And, if you wish, I can read out Article 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We've got all these articles -- it talks about, I agree, about work obligation. But, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours I will allow myself to be sidetracked down this road, but I would ask for the extra time that I -- because this is the General, I think, responding to my request that he -- I identify the law. But I've got a number of other documents I want to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I have only got about half -- well, I've got 35 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: By extra time, you mean the extra 15 minutes that we lost at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. If I'm going to be allowed to side -- if the General wants to make this point, which I can -- he wants me to look at Article 26. And I don't want to stop him because it wouldn't be fair, but I don't actually particularly want to deal with this. I have got other matters that I want to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krgovic could pick that up in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we're at the time for the first break for the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- I notified the Registrar and the Court Officer before the beginning of today that there is a matter I would like to raise concerning the translations. And I -- and together with Ms. Korner, we tried to resolve that situation over the break, but it -- we didn't -- we didn't resolve it. And in the meantime there was another issue of the -- of the -- of the interpretation which I think was not correct in the transcript. So I would need to raise this before the witness leaves, and I don't know whether Your Honours would permit me to do so right now, or would you like me to do that a bit later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- perhaps when Ms. Korner has finished her cross-examination may be a convenient point before Mr. Krgovic begins his re-examination, since it involves the witness who is presently on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is the General has now raised this question of what's in the Law on National Defence, which, I think, was a response to something I put to him yesterday and invited him to look for it. But I do have to deal with it. I cannot let it be dealt with for re-examination because it's quite an important issue. And so I -- I would ask, I'm afraid -- I appreciate that the General has been here for a long time, but these really are major issues, and I would, therefore, ask that I be given added time to deal, I hope fairly shortly, with this thing he has just raised, and then to complete my cross-examination with -- I have another dozen or so documents I want to look at very quickly with him, but that would certainly take the whole of the 35 minutes or so that I have left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, can I, in effect, I'd like another 45 to 50 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You mean in total?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the guillotine will descend 40 minutes after the witness resumes the stand. And while the witness is being escorted back to the stand, on behalf of the chamber, we express our gratitude to CLSS for being able to accommodate at very short notice the extended sitting which we have had to arrange for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the General to come in, could we have document 1 -- L1 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, I want to deal extremely quickly, please, so please keep your answers short, to what you've just raised with me. You directed our attention to the parts of the Law on National Defence which relate to work obligation. Could we have up Article 23, please, at speed. That sets out work obligation, and it talks about the time of war and immediate threat of war, all citizens able to work, blah, blah, blah. Next please could we have Article 24. It's on the screen there. We need to go to the next page in English. "Members of the police and other authorised official persons employed with the internal affairs organs shall carry out their work obligation within the internal affairs organ [sic]." Correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Article 26, please, which is the next -- 26, yes, thank you. "The performance" -- ah sorry, yes, Article 26: "Performance of tasks and duties required by the armed forces and the occasional performance of work significant for the defence of the country shall be ordered by the competent municipal organ. "In time of war if the need for immediate combat action of the armed forces so required and the competent organ is unable to issue tasks [sic]," blah blah. You're reading that article, aren't you that the brigade commander can then take over police?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether that's right or wrong doesn't really matter for these purposes because there was no state of war at this period in 1992, was there? And there's a clear distinction drawn between immediate threat of war and state of war in the original article.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I said that, in my opinion, there are no great differences when it comes to the jurisdiction of the commander in a state of imminent threat of war, on the one hand, and in a state of war on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm wrong, but maybe it's translation issue. It was -- says in this article: "In the war." [Interpretation] The imminent threat of war is not mentioned here. The state of war isn't mentioned, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I fully appreciate it is talking about in time of war, not an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it may be, may it not, General, one of the reasons why General Talic was complaining that a state of war had not been declared and, indeed, as we saw or as we know in 1994, maybe to get round the problems, a state of war was declared? So it does have an illegal effect, doesn't it General? Or if you'd -- I mean, you told us you're not a lawyer, so if you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous article should also be read. That I believe it also mentions the imminent threat of war. And to my mind, the law should be interpreted as a whole. That is why I relied on this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, General, I suggest to you that contrary to what you are asserting these provisions had no effect on the actual -- certainly on the actual reality and indeed as you yourself said, let me just find it, page ... When I was asking you about a document from Mr. Bjelosevic, when you quoted -- no, sorry. Zupljanin document in September. And you said: "Ms. Korner I told you" -- This is it page 20, line 12: "I told you how I interpret the rules and regular legislations [sic]. I can see the practice was different, and I emphasise that in exceptional circumstances the commanders could take people on their own from work duty and transfer them to military duty and in other cases the regulations intend for this to be done by the authorised organ upon the request of the units, military units." And you were referring there, were you not, the authorised organ, to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. The competent municipal organ. I said it was an organ from the defence system, and it has a very wide authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But do you agree that it's clear from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm really sorry. I know Ms. Korner you're pressed, but the witness was starting to -- the -- give the answer, and the part of his answer was not recorded. And I think it's important. He mentioned the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, I'm not at all clear under right Mr. Zecevic keeps standing up. This is not his witness. This is Mr. Krgovic's witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, General, repeat, please, your answer.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is very difficult for me to do that because I, too, am trying to be helpful. Here it says that this is in the remit of the municipal defence organ which is under the Ministry of Defence. I wanted to add that, during a war, conscription has priority over any other duties, and that is clearly stated in various laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But clearly the article we looked at earlier, Article 24, intends that the police shall be, if you like, exempt from this all-encompassing conscription of those under work obligation. Because it says they will do it in the ministry of internal affairs unless, and I suggest that it's quite clear from Article 26, it's talking about if there's an actual time or state of war. And you say you don't agree with that. So that's all I want to deal with you on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move, please, back to what I'm trying to do at considerable speed this morning, and that is look at the documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were shown during the course of your examination-in-chief, or cross-examination, so-called, by Mr. Cvijetic, a document in which General Talic sent to the CSB and the 343rd Brigade, a complaint about deserting soldiers, saying that criminal charges had to be brought. And he was quoting what the Main Staff had apparently told him. And you say that's a clear example that the military dealt well discipline. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember what I said, but I can comment --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't want your comment.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the document with you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you've already commented. I want to show you another document, please. Do you agree that desertion is a military offence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you also agree that failing to obey an order is a military offence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you have a look now, please, at document -- Exhibit 1888, I think. Tab 75C.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if you allow, while we're waiting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, the document's here. This is a document, the 18th of October, which is being sent to the SJB by Stojan Zupljanin to the chief. Looks like it's Gradiska, I think. It starts: "At the request of the 1st Krajina Corps on 12th of October, 107 members of the police," in fact, it's a number of them, "36 from Banja Luka, 35 from Prijedor, 35 from Gradiska, and a senior worker from Banja Luka CSB were resubordinated to the Republika Srpska to carry out specific tasks. On the 17th of October 1992 all 35 workers of Gradiska refused to take any further orders from the officers and voluntarily returned to Gradiska. The chief the CSB ordered on the 17 October that on the morning of the 18th a new police platoon at Gradiska was to be sent to continue the tasks, that all workers who refused to obey orders were suspended, and criminal measures filed against them." Do you accept that it is clear from this, that for this breach of military discipline, it is the police who are taking the disciplinary measures? Or, indeed, criminal measures, in fact.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in this case, these persons were military conscripts, and according to what I say in my report, proceedings should have been instigated by the military commanders to whose contingent these persons belonged --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if this is your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not what's happening, is it, from this document? It's not the military. It's the police who are bringing these charges. Do you agree with that, before I put my next question to you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm trying to see where it states that the police initiated things. But in any case it's better for someone to start things off rather than no one doing it, from the aspect of establishing law and order and determining responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I quite agree. But the point that I'm trying to make to you is that your assertion, which is that only the military could take proceedings because these were military conscripts, is misconceived. And that's because you haven't looked at all the documents.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And I suggest to you that when you say they become military conscripts, they remain, I suggest, policemen who have been resubordinated for the purposes of unity or singleness of command but that if disciplinary proceedings are to be taken, it will be done within their own chain of command. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because, logically, I suggest to you, it would be inconceivable that the military would take these measures, first, because I don't imagine they had any desire to, because it was a lot of administrative work. But, second, because they had no power to remove these people as police officers, did they? Which is the ultimate disciplinary sanction.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, when a person is being transferred from work duty to military duty, their status changes. They receive a different assignment. They received a different coloured paper. And all of that is in force for as long as they are a military person. They are assigned different powers and are responsible along the military line. This is what the military rules and regulations state. And in war time, you cannot interpret it other than like that, because those issues are exclusively under the jurisdiction of military commanders when they are dealing with military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. That is the Defence case and that the case you are putting forward. But my suggestion to you is, logically, how could the military in -- take disciplinary proceedings which meant the removal of a police officer as an authorised official? He couldn't, could he? Only the minister could do that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that person is not a policeman at that point. They are a military conscript. So the question whether they would return to their previous post is something that, again, has to follow procedure, through the authorised organ so that his status could be changed again. And, on the -- in the Law on Military Duty, for which you say has not been seen here but which I did provide, and in Article 111 [as interpreted] it says precisely when somebody starts their military duty and when they end it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I believe the witness said Article 11, and it's recorded 111.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, General. I don't want to get too bogged down in this. Do you have any explanation then why, on the face of this document, Zupljanin is saying that the chief of the Banja Luka CSB ordered, firstly, a new police platoon; and, secondly, criminal measures to be filed against them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't want to comment this particular case. I'm talking about the rules and regulations and what they state and how it should have been done. I personally agree that this is something that should have been sanctioned and that it's better that someone did it, rather than no one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You're talking about your interpretation of rules and regulations of which you have no idea of their application to the VRS or the MUP during 1992. That's correct, isn't it? You simply don't know what happened in practice.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we look now, please, quickly at document number 76, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Ms. Korner, but I'm confused. I think you put two questions to me just previously. Perhaps one should have had the answer yes and the other one no, if I have a right to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot think so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I see that, yes. You're going to say, yes, it's your interpretation; and, no, you don't know about -- and you agree that you don't know what happened in practice. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now, perhaps Ms. Korner needs to put the questions again, because now this is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. You can re-examine. Yes. All right. Directive 4, very quickly, please. That's not Directive 4. P1780.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this deals with the -- the police brigade that you were again only shown one document about. Have you seen -- no, I don't think you've seen this before. This is the directive that was issued by the Main Staff in respect of further operations. And, in fact, I don't think we need to look at it because, I beg your pardon, what comes out of it is what is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at the next document. The date of Directive 4 was the 19th of November. So could we have a look now, please, at document P1668, Your Honours, which is under seal - it's tab 77 - and therefore shouldn't go out on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated 21st of November, two days later. It's from Talic to Zupljanin. It's headed: Engaging the Unit in Combat Activities." And then: "In accordance with expressed needs our detailed assessment, the requirement to remain [sic] the existing corridor ..." et cetera. "It's our opinion that the engagement of strong forces from your units would be necessary and unavoidable." And then in the third paragraph: "We therefore ask you to immediately begin preparing, organising, and establishing police units ..." Do you go the word is "ask"? It's not "order," it's "ask"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it says both. First, it says we ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you read out the --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Read out -- read out the whole paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We ask you to immediately begin preparing, organising, and establishing police units with a strength of at least two battalions, and more, if possible."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And you say it says both. Where is the word "order"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the word "molimo vas," we ask you to immediately begin. Then this would be the tone of an order that relates to preparing, organising, and establishing, and it determines precisely the strength. It's possible that it's something that's being asked -- that is being asked regarding the strength and the preparations themselves. It's difficult for me to interpret this document of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I agree that it's not fair to ask you that. Can we look, please, at the next document then in this whole series which led up to the January document that you were shown by the Defence. Could we look, please, at 2D119, also under seal, so not on the screen. Not on the public screen. 22nd of November, so the following day, Zupljanin -- yep. Zupljanin issues the order because it's gone from the minister, he says: "In accordance with the order of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska ... on the basis of a dispatch from the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps ..." And that's the one that we've just looked at because it's got that number, 730192. So clearly Talic has sent this to minister, copied it Zupljanin, and the minister has now given him the order. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, this is unfair because if Ms. Korner is showing the document of Talic referring to the document, she must refer to the order of the minister as well. That is the document from 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why do I have to show it to him again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But that that document precedes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I accept that entirely. Yes, I see -- okay. I see the point Mr. Zecevic is making. I said that the order has gone from Talic to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is based on the minister's order of the 15th of May and the document has gone from Talic to Zupljanin who then makes this order. I accept that. Do you see there that in fact at this stage of the game the person who is appointed to command this police brigade, which I fully accept, General, was resubordinated properly to the 1st Krajina Corps. Do you see that the commander was a gentleman named Brane Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was in fact -- who was in fact, and the Court knows this, was a member of the MUP. Right. And then what then happens, we can see, is -- well, what we know is that Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic gets -- replaces Mr. Pecanac, and then he is replaced in the one document that the Defence showed you in January, by this other military officer. Now, can we look next, please, at 1D172. I can't remember whether you were shown this document or not, General. Have you seen this document before? This is the establishment of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I think that the document is there, in the description of my work. I'm not sure, but I would have to check.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry. I'm not -- [indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because earlier I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Anyhow, all I want to ask you about is this. Article 2 says who the Supreme Command is: The president, the supreme commander of the Presidency, national assembly, prime minister, national defence, and the minister of the interior. Would you agree that this is an attempt to try and, as it were, pull together what was effectively the reality of the situation, that the minister of the interior, during the course of 1992, had the power to refuse to give his men to the army and, therefore, it was decided to pass this law?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which law are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Decision, sorry. I beg your pardon, decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Make this decision.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this is a decision on the forming of the Supreme Command, and I don't understand why we're talking about the powers of the minister of the interior. I cannot just put that in the context that you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- would wish for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to think of a reason why, when, according to you, the minister of the interior should -- had no power to -- to make any orders in respect of the army, he should now suddenly become part of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I think that the Supreme Commander commands the army on behalf of the Supreme Command, not the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think I made my point. Moving on, speedily, please. Can we look now, please, at the MUP report for the year 1992, P625. Can we look, please, at - one, two, three -- fourth page in English. And fifth page, I think, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do we see -- actually, you need to go to the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The activities of police employees from the beginning of the armed conflict varied from one station to another. For example: "Employees in police stations in Bihac," et cetera, et cetera, "joined in the combat activities from the outset whilst other municipalities where there was less fighting, or it began later, the police at first began to carry out their regular tasks and duties which included disarming groups --" and I'm sorry. Doesn't say "which included," I'm suggesting that's what it says. "Disarming groups, finding and seizing weapons, and when the need arose they joined the Army of the Republika Srpska. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It makes a distinction, does it not, with their regular duties which included disarming groups, unspecified, and then when the need arose, joining the RS, I suggest -- the VRS, as resubordinated police officers?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think I need more about this. Now, I want to look, please, finally at the 1994 law that you were shown by Mr. Cvijetic. And this is Defence tab 16, L317. I say "finally." I do have three more documents on other aspects I want to put to you, but this is the last one on the topic of resubordination. This is Decree on the Promulgation of the Law on the Implementation of the Law on Ministries During an Imminent Threat of War or a State of War, and I think agreed with Mr. Cvijetic, this was to regularise, wasn't it, and incorporate into a law the various earlier laws and practice of what had happened. Would you agree with that? I think you did agree with that with Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree, if that is I what I said about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to look at, please, with you, the law of -- first one what you looked at, the Law on Implementation of the Defence, Article 2, the armed forces include the units of the Ministry of Interior. And then can we look, please, at the -- the implementation on the Law of Affairs [sic], please, which is page 9 of the English. Is that what's showing?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could somebody please indicate to me where it is in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4; and in the English, it's page 9, Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Not interested in Article 4. "Procedures to be adopted by the ministry. The ministry may take the following measures."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it's setting out the procedures that the ministry of internal affairs will take in those circumstances; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Move on, please, to the next part, 3: "Responsibility of ministry personnel." Disciplinary measures -- Article 9, sorry. "Disciplinary measures shall be imposed by the Ministry of Interior [sic] or a person authorised by him." It then sets out what the punishments shall be, that -- what the sanctions will be, and says in Article 11: "Disciplinary proceedings issued before this law entered into force shall be completed according to the provisions of this law." Then the next part is the use of police in combat operations. Article 12 through to 17. Which is really, to a large extent, reincorporating Article 104 and adding to that article about what happens to the police. But nowhere does it say that the minister's right to conduct disciplinary proceedings does not apply when members of the MUP are resubordinated, does it, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, Ms. Korner, I don't have the whole law in front of me. But I still maintain that in situations when police units are subordinated to a military commander and become military conscripts, then that would be under the jurisdiction of the military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know you keep asserting it, and I know that's what the Defence case is. But, surely, General, even you will admit that in a law that was passed to make it abundantly clear what the relationship between the MUP and the army was, they would have said, Disciplinary proceedings will be conducted by the minister unless resubordination has taken place, in which case, it is the army?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you were allowed an extra five minutes to accommodate the loading of documents and the other interruptions, but your time is now expired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the greatest respect, I really would ask that I be allowed -- because there have been a number of assertions which I have not covered -- I have at least -- I would ask at least that I can put two more documents because we've not covered at all the -- the -- the Crisis Staffs. Your Honours, I haven't reached the 20 hours I asked for. I knew this would be a lengthy cross-examination. I did not realise, of course, that I would have to spend so much time on his report and the sources. But, Your Honour, that is important. Whatever the Defence may complain about, because of the submissions I shall be making at the end, which I tried to make in the middle. Your Honours, I would ask that I be allowed to put these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, you told Mr. Cvijetic that during the course of your examination of documents you had looked at documents relating to Crisis Staffs. They do not appear in your bibliography, they did not appear in any of the lists of the Defence -- well, I'm sorry, your bibliography for the report. So can we take it that you did not look at any documents when preparing your report that were issued but the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you, however, because in relation to town commands, you've made various assertions that they are set up by a military officer, and it's entirely him who sets them up. I want you to look, please, at a document, P448, which is at tab 55.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In English, could we look, please, at the third page; and in B/C/S, it is page ... the third page, I think. No, bottom -- yes, that page. Bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These are the books of minutes that were kept by the Kljuc Crisis Staff and there they set out -- it's on 27th of May, the relationship between the military and civilian authorities shall be as follows. The military authorities will follow the orders of the civilian authorities. The civilian authorities will not interfere with the way they are followed. Although it's -- it's rather pre-emptory put, that, in fact, is right, isn't it? Because it was the political element that set the goals and it was for the military to carry out those goals. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner, if you're referring to that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, can we look next, please, at document -- sorry, page 3 of this document in English -- oh, sorry, two pages on in English. And it's -- the trouble is this was labelled very badly, Your Honours, in the original. In the B/C/S, it's -- it says, 38 -- it's got no page number so I can't tell. It says 3003 or 500573884 -- 883, sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is meeting of the 29th of May. And it says, under the session the following was concluding [sic] that a defence command should be set up and that Major Bosko Lukic should be appointed a commander. Its commander. Do you accept that from this document the Crisis Staff is making the decision that a town command should be set up? A defence command it's called, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as far as I remember, I said that, according to the laws and regulations, defence commands shall be set up. That is mostly done in a situation when the authorities in the area concerned are not functional, or when the situation demands that all forces be integrated and put under the command of the defence commander. And I cannot see from this who it is that's supposed to do that, to set it up. The commander of the defence command is directly appointed by the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I know that's what you say. And can I say I accept entirely town commands came into existence when the civilian authorities were unable to function. However, here, it would appear, that the defence -- the municipal Crisis Staff of which, I don't know whether you know that, the SJB chief, the military -- the local military chief, were all members. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the town command includes all the organs in the area. I'm talking about what the theory says and how it should be. I don't know how it really was in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, here, the Kljuc Crisis Staff is saying the defence command should look [sic] up, and can we look, please, finally, and that is the last document I want you to look at, is at document P1783, at tab 29. The meeting of the Kljuc Crisis Staff that we looked at was the 29th of May. On the 31st of May, we have Colonel Galic putting into effect the order or the request of the -- the Kljuc Crisis Staff and setting up the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where is in this document? Where is mentioned in this document? Or is this suggestion by Ms. Korner, because it is not what is in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand Mr. Krgovic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where does the document say that the commander is implementing the decision of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
