utterances.text: It's my suggestion. On the 31st -- 29th of May, and I -- on the 29th of May, the Kljuc orders -- municipal Crisis Staff orders that a defence command be set up. On the 31st of May, Colonel Galic sets up a defence command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With the assistance of Mr. Krgovic, are you going to say, General, that these two events are not connected?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, these two events are -- probably are connected, but it's the division commander here who decides about setting up a defence command of the town. He is the superior commander of the brigade commander. It is not logical for the president of the municipal assembly who was in power should take a decision to renounce power and transfer himself to another organ where a military officer would be his commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The situation is this, isn't it: That where there was a complete breakdown of civilian authority for as short a period as possible - and I haven't got time to show other documents, but that's evident - what's called a town or defence command was set up. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as soon as it was possible for the normal civilian, that is to say, municipal presidents, police and the like, to function, the town command was abolished?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. General, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, before you begin, you would recall that Mr. Zecevic, there is a matter that he raised with which he wanted to deal. General, we're near time for the break, but there is an short procedural matter with which we have to deal so I would ask the usher to escort you out a little ahead of us. And we would resume in 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Your Honours, yesterday, during the cross-examination of this witness, on pages 63, line 1, to 68, line 1, Ms. Korner was suggesting to the witness when reading from the document, which is 1D46 -- if we can have that document up, please. Ms. Korner suggested to the witness that the -- that the wording of the document says that means -- that the word "may" means that it is not given that police forces will be used. "It is within the authority of the minister or the chiefs of the CSB." Your Honours, the problem is that this is wholly erroneous interpretation and misleading to the witness. We didn't want to raise it, because, at the time when it was -- when the question was asked, because it would be -- it might be perceived as we are trying to coach the witness. But this is an important thing, Your Honours, and it's very illustrative of the -- of the problems that -- that might develop further on where Your Honours are going to determine the issues in this case, and the understanding of our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor; namely, linguistic interpretation of the meaning of the word is done from the translation, as opposed that it's done from the original. From the original, Your Honours, it is very clear, it's at paragraph 7 that I'm talking about. Paragraph 7, first page. It is -- it is very clear from the Serbian language that the word "may" is used to -- to state the authority of the persons who are entitled to take that decision. It has nothing to do with their understanding, as Ms. Korner is putting, whether -- whether it's given that the police will be used or -- or that they have any -- any -- any doubts about that. It is just that the -- that the word "moze," m-o-z-e, in Serbian language, is used as "can," as "may." There is no distinction. So the question that is answered in this paragraph 7 is: Who can order the use of the police forces in combat? And it says: "The use of the police in combat can be ordered, or may be ordered by ..." Therefore, it strictly, from the -- from -- from the Serbian language, it's strictly, and there is no doubt about it whatsoever, that this refers to the persons, the three persons, the minister, the commander of a special brigade in the case of the CSB Sarajevo, and the other CSB officers. Therefore, I -- I -- I'm just raising this because this is a -- this is a problem which we will be facing when -- when -- when we are -- when we are coming down to the actual presentation of -- of our final submissions. And this is, in my opinion, a relatively big problem, and I'm not sure what is the -- what is the -- the best way how to -- to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may inject a measure of confusion, Mr. Zecevic. I refrained yesterday, when Ms. Korner was pursuing this, from making the observation that, apart from the inherent difficulty of dealing with the interpretation from one language to another, even among English speakers in the construction of statues, the word "may" is confusing because whereas ordinarily it is permissive, there are occasions in which "may" is mandatory. So it struck me at the time, and from what you have said today I am reinforced in that view, that this is a matter ripe for argumentation, and no doubt at the appropriate time the Chamber is going to have the benefit - and I use that term advisedly - of submissions from both sides to the extent that anything turns on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say, we did try to reach agreement, but there's, I'm afraid, for Your Honours -- the reasons that Your Honour has already articulated, those that I consulted who -- who are native speakers of the language, didn't wholly agree with Mr. Krgovic's interpretation of it. And as I said, of course, it is Stanisic's right not to give evidence, but in the end, the only person who can explain what he meant by that order is the minister himself. And as Your Honour has said, the rest is for argument and what follows and that will be the difference between the two of us. Now, the second -- I believe Mr. Zecevic has another matter that he wanted to raise on interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, today, at page -- I'm sorry. Page 19, line 23. The witness was shown the document - just bear with me Your Honour, one second - it's document P1094. And then a part of it was read to the -- to the witness. And -- or it was -- Ms. Korner was asking the witness to read the part of the -- of that document. And the witness says, 19, 23: "I think here Mr. Zupljanin, and it says: 'I kindly ask the corps commander to draw the attention of the lower-ranking commands.'" Then Ms. Korner: "Could you pause there for a moment. The word 'kindly' doesn't appear in the English translation. Where does that appear?" "Interpreter's correction: I ask."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Thank you." Your Honours, the word is "molim." The word is "molim." It is: "I kindly ask." Now, Ms. Korner is using -- Ms. Korner is using this document to show the relationship between Mr. Zupljanin and the corps commander. The nature of the relationship --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Korner. Trying to show the -- the relationship between the two persons. And in my opinion, this might create a different understanding than it is in the document itself. It's, again, Your Honours, with all due respect, the same problem as I -- as I -- as I stated before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So unless I'm missing something, is this -- does this have to be referred back for translation? Or, again, is this a matter which will be left to argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but all means, it needs to be re-sent back to CLSS to retranslate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You don't resist that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, in fact, funnily enough, my understanding of the word "molim," which I have heard on a number of occasions, is it means "please." But I think if there is a dispute, and it's a Defence document, it needs to go back for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So ordered. So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I would remind you that we would be adjourning at 1.30, with a view to reconvening at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us return to the last topic you discussed with Ms. Korner, and that was the town command, or defence command of Kljuc. You then said who was authorised to take that decision, and in connection with that, let us take a look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's -- please bear with me. 65 ter 2025.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 20225. That's tab 12 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, this, according to the Prosecution, is from the 1st Krajina Corps. It says: "Duty team." Please look at page 78 in the Serbian. And it's on pages 59 and 60 in English. There's an entry here, paragraph 2: "The commander decided to set up a special command for the defence of Kljuc and the entire municipality, which is to comprise," and he is now listing the units and the control of the area. And it goes on to say that another battalion is to be set up from the Kljuc area to be deployed in the area of Krasulje, Ramici, Kamicak and some independent companies and police are included there. General, this is a document from the corps command. Can you please comment on these authorities, or authorisations, as -- about which you spoke to Ms. Korner. And what is the relationship between this battalion and the part where the police is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, this document confirms what I said to Ms. Korner, that the military commander decides about setting up town commands. He determines the structures and forces, all of which in conditions when the authorities are not functional. All forces are then under the command of the town command commander, and they're all subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say that another battalion is to be set up from the area of Kljuc and there are some independent companies and police. What about these independent companies and police with regard to paragraph 26 of the Law on All People's Defence? Could you please comment on this paragraph, bearing that in mind.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the police mentioned here is subordinated to the commander of the town defence command. This is a direct resubordination of all forces, not only the police, in that area. This police here, if that's what you mean, has the status of subordinated unit with regard to the commander of the town defence command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you another paragraph from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before we leave this document, could we be shown on the screen the date of this entry? Which is on the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is 30 May. I apologise, I wanted to show the first page, but I don't know the page reference for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page -- yes, here you see it, it's 30 May. And now let's see page 13 in the Serbian and 11 in the English. General, Ms. Korner showed you this document in the context of information and the functioning of communications, as well as the good functioning of the corps, or corps. And I'll read out this paragraph and these are supposed to be the words of Major Kojic. It says: "A generally disorganised situation. "Every TO staff runs a separate operation. "Second Lieutenant Dabic and the lieutenant from the special purpose unit working according to a plan of their own. "I cannot go on like this, I am asking for someone to come here and co-ordinate all this because I feel like leaving. "There is no communication with anyone. "A single command should be established and all actions co-ordinated, otherwise, this will all come to nothing." General, this document of the 1st Krajina Corps, what does it say about the general situation in Republika Srpska, to your mind?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, when I was writing my report and making my assertions, I don't want to quote wrongly now, but the foundation for my assertions is, first and foremost, the analysis of combat readiness of the VRS, where at several places there is talk about the problems with the functioning. There was a section about morale, as far as I remember, another section about communications, the poor training level of the force, the failure of officers from Serbia to arrive, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when Ms. Korner asked you about some of the things you said in the introductory part, you referred several times to analysis of combat readiness. General, are you able to tell us so that we would all know, what is an analysis of combat readiness? What does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, an analysis of combat readiness is one of the compulsory activities of the units and commands at all levels. It is carried out at the end of the calendar year, and it's a summary by specifically determined questions, as well as an analysis before that of the overall situation in the army, pursuant to pre-set elements of combat readiness. And this is something that is used to this day in all the armies, and the top state leadership is informed about its conclusions, if we're talking about the top level, where an analysis of the entire army is carried out. So it's a statement of the status, the problems, the way to resolve the problems, relationships, organisational issues, and numerous other issues. It deals with -- it usually ends with conclusions, assignments to subordinated units, as well as a proposal for measures relating to the superior command. And, in this instance, this refers to the state leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, if we wanted to see what the situation was in a specific army, in a specific time-period, what the problems were, what the situation was, which document would be the best used for such a purpose?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, it would be this precise document. And that's why it's always given the highest confidentiality classification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the analysis of combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Krgovic. I was thinking of the analysis of the combat readiness of a command, a unit, and its importance grows with the levels of command that it covers. The higher the level, the greater the importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, now I'm going to show you 01071, tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Krgovic. General, the -- one -- one of your answers to Mr. Krgovic -- "as well as a proposal for measures related to superior command. And in this instance this refers to state leadership." Is this -- when you say "state leadership," do I understand you to mean political leadership, as contrasted with the highest military leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we're talking about an analysis of combat readiness of the highest military level, I meant that the proposed measures would be submitted to the top. In this specific case, to the president of the republic as the Supreme Commander. And that is something that is the -- the commander's duty and the Main Staff to submit this to the supreme commander, i.e., the president, once a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And do I correctly infer when, in one of your earlier answers, you talked about the -- I think you used the word "elements" against which the performance is measured, this is also set by the leadership at that level. Am I correct in that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the elements of combat readiness that are being analysed and used to develop the rules are set by the rules and regulations. For example, number one would be the control -- command and control; number two would be level of training; number three would be morale; four would be personnel policies; five would be logistics and so on and so forth. There's no need for me to mention all the details. These are pre-set elements, set by the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you mentioned earlier that there are analyses of combat readiness at different levels. In this analysis of combat readiness of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, which information from subordinated units is this report supposed to contain? Are these their analyses, are there separate reports, or is it something completely different?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, before the analysis, analyses are carried out by the commands in the units for lower-ranking units. Before this analysis, the command of the corps analyses are completed. And in this analysis would include all the results and the situation represented in the analyses of lower-ranking commands. So this is how it proceeds, all the way up to the battalion command. Analyses have to be conducted in their own commands and units before they go up to the next level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, Ms. Korner put a lot of questions to you from your introduction, and she showed you a series of documents about the functioning of the former JNA and the relationship of the JNA during a certain time-period and its combat readiness. So I would like to ask you: In the analysis on page 9 in the Serbian and 8 in the English, if we can just comment on one particular passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second paragraph from the top, please. Command and control sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It states: "Intelligence and reconnaissance activities were organised in keeping with our capacities, although we had very limited resources after the collapse of the control and command system of the 2nd Military District of the former JNA." General, are you able to tell us what this 2nd Military District was? What did it cover.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Military District, as far as I can remember, was headquartered in Sarajevo, and it covered a significant area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In respect of your assertions in your previous testimony, when the JNA, as it was withdrawing from Croatia and Slovenia, at the same time was falling apart, and in light of that information, are you able to comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, could I have an exact reference to that answer? Page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours I'm able to do that at the break. Yesterday the witness was answering these questions, so I was just speaking generally. He talked about the withdrawal and the falling apart of the JNA. I will find the references. He did mention that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But I think he is able to comment on this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, as far as I can remember, and I know, that I said that the Yugoslav People's Army from Slovenia to Bosnia and Herzegovina was gradually falling apart, that people stayed in their republics, that numerous materiel and equipment also remained in these republics, and I think that this fits in with this assessment here from the combat readiness analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last paragraph where it says: "Order and discipline are not at the required level, although we did introduce temporary regulations --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We need the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page in the Serbian and the next -- page 9 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "There are adequate laws on defence and the army, but this was not implemented in some units. The combat [as interpreted] of soldiers in some units is not always pursuant to the regulations in effect, although there are major differences from unit to unit." And then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what's come out on the screen -- sorry, and the translation, it was quite difficult to hear, but it says "the combat of soldiers in some units." I think what should be there is "conduct."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. [Interpretation] Yes, it says here the conduct of soldiers. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then you have the fourth paragraph from the top, where certain failings are pointed out. And it says: "Individual --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters need a reference in the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, could you give the interpreters a reference to the English text because they don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 10; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, it says: "Command and control was particularly influenced by the lack of adequate senior cadre at the level of companies and battalions. Considerable reserves, according to some officers of active officers, and the links of units to their home territory, desertion, and incomplete execution of the mobilisation ..." General, let's now look at your introduction. This is page 3 in the Serbian version, paragraph 2. And you comment there, you were answering questions about this by Ms. Korner, when you wrote this introduction. Can you please tell me what the purpose of the introduction was. Was it your intention to deal with these matters in detail, the beginning of the war, the introduction ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, I [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [In English] I rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I apologise. What was your intention in writing this introduction?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, when I wrote this introduction, all I wanted, and as I did state in the introduction, was to place my work in the context of the conditions prevailing at the time or in the context of the situation at the time in the Army of Republika Srpska on the basis of their conclusions and to point out to the difficulties and problems that existed in that initial period of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to this document, P1781. Can we now have page 27, please, in the Serbian version, and page 30 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You answered a lot of questions by Ms. Korner about the information that I read to you earlier on. On page 23994 of the transcript, you said that, lines 11, you said that this was a basis for your analysis of combat readiness, and in several places, page 24012, you also refer to that source of information, and several times, these things that I found quickly. So I want to draw your attention to this part about the communications system in the Army of Republika Srpska. I'm going to show you this paragraph. It's the second paragraph from the top. It states: "From the very beginning of the war, and with its further escalation, the stationary part of the system of communications of the former JNA was disrupted, as well as the communications of other operators." And then in parentheses they are mentioned. It's the post office, the MUP, television, radio, power generation and distribution, enterprises, and railways, as well as the power generation and transmission systems suffered major damage, and part of the war weaponry and equipment of the communications corps left in the territory of the opponent. And then it goes on to say: "The mobile section of the communication system was also considerably disrupted by the move of parts of and some entire signals units of the former JNA into the Army of Yugoslavia." And then it goes on to say: "The greatest problem faced by the signals body of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in planning and organising communications was the breakdown of the stationary segment of the communications system, especially of some vital facilities Bjelasnica, Zlovrh and Vlasic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to move to the next page; page 28. And this would be page 31 in the English. Page 28 in the Serbian; 31 in the English. I'm sorry, there is some sort of discrepancy between the English and the Serbian versions. Could you please scroll up this first page, where it says: "From the previous diagram you can see ..." Actually, I think it's one page back in the English; I apologise. You can see that from a total of 16 communications nodes, five of them -- yes. That is the one, the paragraph-but-last in the English version. "16" -- "the above diagram shows that of a total of 16 stationary communications hubs, five of them ... were abandoned and left in enemy territory, while one stationary communications hub ... was seized by the enemy ..." Can you scroll down, please, so I can see the end of the paragraph. "No less of a problem for" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters need a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, once again, the interpreters ask for a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. [Interpretation] It goes on to say, and the page of the English translation is -- lower down. Could we scroll down in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "In planning and establishing a new organisation of communications, the considerably disrupted system of stationary communications centres and auxiliary communication centres of the former JNA, posed no less a problem. Of a total of 32 facilities, 11 were abandoned or captured and three were damaged ..." And there's another page, General, that deals with communications, and given this combat readiness analysis, please explain to us your introductory section where you speak about poor communications.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, that is exactly what I had in mind when I stated my assessments. Even more so, since it's well known that the communications system is the most important foundation, or one of the most important elements, for good command and control of units and formations for successful transmission of orders, as well as successful reporting, bottom-up reporting. If this system is disrupted, as we can see in this analysis, then the conditions for all activities between the commands and units are much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you spoke extensively about the setting up of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 13 in both linguistic versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "The infantry units which through self-organisation grew on a massive scale out of the Territorial Defence and other units, were used only at the beginning of the war according to the decisions of the Crisis Staffs and similar authoritative bodies. Among the infantry units there were also units which represented various political structures, which were sometimes in opposition to the overall objectives of our war." General, it says: "... sometimes in opposition to the overall objectives of our war." In your report you also touched upon these topics and you mentioned improvisation, if I remember correctly. Can you comment on this section?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, these are only some of the significant problems pointed out in this analysis, and I took them into consideration when I wrote about the organisation of the VRS, its level of training, and its overall functioning, especially during the initial period of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On page 24012 of the transcript, line 6 through 11, Ms. Korner asked you to give an example of a private commanding a unit, and you said that it could be found in the analysis of combat readiness. Please take a look at page 71 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's paragraph 4.3, 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph says: "A large number of the officer establishment posts have been filled with soldiers who, by their courage, resolution [as interpreted] and professionalism have won for themselves positions of leadership and even command."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's go to the following page, which is 72 in the Serbian version. It's the third paragraph here, which discusses a similar topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "So far this problem has been addressed by assigning non-commissioned officers and brave and able soldiers, mostly from blue collar occupations, to the mentioned establishment posts. Although they are discharging their duties successfully and capably, they cannot be promoted to the rank of officer." And when you were answering Ms. Korner's question about these instances, what did you have in mind when you had to give a specific example?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krgovic, I meant the allegations in this analysis. It is well-known that there must be four years' education to be appointed to an officer's position, but these were conditions of war. The situation was the way it was, and this is how it was assessed in their analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, speaking about these things, on page 23984, lines 9 through 19, you said about a footnote that there was a mistake in your reference. I wanted to correct that, but Ms. Korner didn't allow me. Please take a look at your report now. Paragraph 93. You were -- provide a citation at footnote 43. And I will now show you footnote 44, which is 57D2; that's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm now confused. My understanding was the only footnote that the General said was a mistake he corrected was in relation to the -- the number of the Law on All People's Defence. I know you got up at this stage and said there was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Ms. Korner. While you were examining, the witness said on page 9 that the footnote was -- had a wrong number. I offered to give the correct number of the footnote, but I couldn't, so I have to do it with the witness now. 57D2; that's a 65 ter number. The following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you are dealing with a command here, and you say that it's a continuous process which --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the reference, please, when counsel is reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's in paragraph 93 of your work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 93 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that this is footnote 43. Actually, it is footnote 44. Did you mean that when you said you had made a mistake on page 23984?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you were asked a number of questions in the previous session about when a person becomes a military conscript, and you provided an interpretation of the relevant provisions of the Law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 1D264 to the witness. I think that the Defence -- or the tab in the Defence binder is 117. Let us enlarge, please. 92; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "I have understood your proposal regarding the withdrawal of police forces from combat operations. We are satisfied with the work of the police ... thus far, and we have decided to pull them out for a short while for rest so that we may engage them in upcoming operations. The reasons you provided are valid, but it seems to us that you do not comprehend the situation we are in. I do not authorise the withdrawal of the police ..." General, bearing in mind the authority, or the powers, he has under Article 26 of the Law on All People's Defence -- or I go about it another way. Could you please comment on Colonel Lisica's document in relation to Articles 24 through 26 of the law that you commented on for Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I can tell from the content of this document that the police units are subordinated to this commander and that he is deciding about their use. That is why he explicitly does not authorise their return. Such -- and similar examples I tried to interpret in relation to the aforementioned articles of the Law on All People's Defence, which articles deal with the execution of work obligation, material obligation, the obligation to serve in civilian protection, and military conscription. Under these provisions, the commanders were able to take such decisions, depending on the situation, but I also said that this should not be the usual practice, but, rather, an exception. However, they did have the right to act that way. They had the power to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, we heard what you said. Did Mr. Bjelosevic have the right to withdraw his units? Did he have the power to do so?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, it is my opinion, and I claim that Mr. Bjelosevic did not have that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's convenient time for the break, it's 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take a break now. And we resume at 2.30, we'll sit until 4.00. And then from 4.30 to 6.00, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the last part of the cross-examination, the Prosecutor showed you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P01094, tab 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown the first portion of the document and you commented on it with me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Krgovic please be asked to speak up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The interpreters are concerned that they can't hear you, so if you could please speak up a bit. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you discussed this document with Ms. Korner. This last sentence which reads: "I would kindly ask the corps commander [as interpreted] to draw the attention of their subordinate commands through their own lines." When answering a question by Ms. Korner you said this was a plea by Mr. Zupljanin addressed to the corps commander. Can you please explain the difference in our language between a plea and a request.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, when you make a plea, when you say, Could you please, or May I please ask you, it's something that people with good manners often do. That is often the case. Nevertheless, this is a war situation. A difference between a plea and a request also tells us about the relationship between the two people. If you make a plea to someone, you say, May I please ask you, it is also possibly indicative of your inferior position. If you make a request, that is something to do if you are in a superior position. For example, in terms of rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, in light of what the witness has just explained to us, and, notably, with regard to the comments made by the Presiding Judge before the lunch break, I don't think that we need to go any further into this issue about whether it means one or the other thing. I think it's clear to us what's going on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at page 23757 and onwards, I showed you this document and I asked you to comment in the light of practice. There was the protest by Mr. Zupljanin about the way the police were used. A question for you, sir: We know what the powers were, as you defined them, and we know the Law on Defence. In keeping with those, what if a commander of a certain unit, battalion level or higher up, as you suggested, were to change the status of the members of a certain unit, based on the practical needs, in keeping with the provisions of this article. What about a public security station chief or an official like that? Would they be in a position to refuse this? What would be the status of that particular act produced by the battalion or brigade commander? What his relationship be vis-a-vis these persons?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, if the law endows a military commander with the possibility or, indeed, the right to change the status of a person who is under a work obligation, and changes that status into the status of a military conscript, in that situation, a police chief would be in no position to oppose. The police chief may be unhappy about it, and might even be right to be unhappy about something like that because if you change someone's status like that and you turn a police officer with a work assignment, a work obligation into a military conscript, what that means is that the military conscript might as well remain there for the remaining duration of the war, which means that person is no longer in a position or, indeed, able to perform his tasks. That is how I, for my part, interpret the discontent, dissatisfaction, or, as you say, the protest lodged by the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness please be shown exhibit 65 ter 479D1. It's a Stanisic Defence document. Tab 120. It's a Zupljanin Defence document. My apologies. It's from the Stanisic list, but it's at tab 120 of the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you see the document. It's a corps command document signed by the chief, Mr. Talic. It reads: "Engagement and co-ordination TO units. Warning." There is a translation mistake there. It reads: "Co-ordination" and it should be "co-ordinated action," because the original reads "sadejstvo." That is what we decided, term "co-ordinated action," with TO units. As you said, General, there were some problems regarding this. The document begins like this. It's the -- it's a document by the corps command and delivered to the 5th Brigade, the command of the 5th Brigade. Could you please have a read, sir. The introduction reads: "In combat operations so far and in the resubordination and co-ordination between JNA and TO forces in the zone of responsibility of the 5th Corps, there have been different interpretations ..." And could you please read Article 1.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I quote: "All TO units and staffs in the zone of responsibility of JNA brigades shall be resubordinated to these commands."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, please. Rather, paragraph 2; my apologies.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I quote: "A decision on the engagement and use of TO units shall be taken by the commander of the unit to which the TO unit has been attached, after consultation and agreement with the appropriate officer of the TO unit in question."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, paragraph 3 reads: "JNA brigade commanders shall consider any attached TO units and any other reinforcing units as elements of their own combat deployment and shall take care of these units by providing food and making sure to make proper use of them."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can Mr. Krgovic please be asked to speak up. We cannot hear him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite obvious that I can't pull the mic up which means that I will have to bend a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please comment on this document in the light of your discussion today and on the previous days with Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I realise that this document was only sent to a single unit, the 5th Infantry Brigade. I suppose that, in the sector of its zone of responsibility, there were some irregularities, such as occurrences of dual command. For this reason, I assume the commander issued a warning, emphasizing, in clear and precise terms, who would be resubordinated to whom, who would be responsible to whom, all of which is in keeping with the principles of singleness of command and unity of command, as well as the principle of subordination, which is a principle that is preponderant and valid in any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, the brigade commander here says that the attached units shall henceforth be considered and other reinforcing units. What about these reinforcing units? What could that be? Could that be the TO, could that be some other units?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reinforcing units could also be tactical groups, or even police units being resubordinated to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what about this sentence, what does it mean: "... shall consider as elements of their own combat deployment..." such and such units. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, this means that you can move them around within your own unit. They are now elements of your own combat deployment. You are free to use them as you see fit and as you decide for missions that these elements of the combat deployment would normally be considered suitably trained for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in the case at hand, we have members of some subordinated units, units of the TO, or what are called reinforcing units who, for example, commit a crime or a disciplinary infraction. Who would be in charge of initiating proceedings against these persons?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, this would be the sole responsibility of the brigade in question or the -- of the commander of the brigade in question or the commander of whatever unit we're talking about because all of the individual members are subordinated to the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible for someone else other than the commander to initiate proceedings against these persons? I mean someone who is not part of the chain of command, strictly speaking.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, as for what we see here in this document, and as for what the rules say, this is solely the responsibility of that unit's commander, and no one else. I can't say definitely. I think there are probably some situations where that too might be possible. But if this official is physically there, if he is present in the unit or in the reinforcing unit, it would be the sole responsibility of that unit's commander. He would be in charge of initiating any proceedings and punishing any disciplinary infractions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My question was about the precise point in time at which they were resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, I did understand your question, and that is why I corrected myself by saying at the time. During their resubordination to the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner showed you the document, and she pointed out she believed your interpretation to not be correct. Do you stand by your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't follow that. Which document? I didn't show him this document. I've never seen it before in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous document. That's what I mean. I meant the CSB document concerning disciplinary infractions and punishment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krgovic, I stand by my position as uttered some minutes ago. I believe I also phrased it the same way in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this document please be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you asked the witness to read out the document, which he did. And I thought that you asked him to do so because you wanted to have the contents of that order on the record in order not to submit it for -- into evidence. And now you're asking for the admission -- could I suggest, in light of the enormous time pressure that we're under this afternoon, that you do either one or the other but not both, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, also, I'm sorry, I don't see how this document is relevant. Mr. Krgovic is trying to suggest -- and the General said it may be the police, but there is not one iota of evidence to suggest that this is anything other than a document dealing with resubordination of TO units to the 1st Krajina Corps, and it is pure speculation and guess-work that other reinforcing units, as, indeed, the General said, is police. Nor does it assist, on the face of it, with who is responsible for disciplinary proceedings where the resubordinated brigade of the police are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document is relevant, especially in the light of yesterday's cross-examination by the OTP. They were talking about attaching units and resubordinating units. And it is not subordination that is implied, that was her position yesterday and this document shows otherwise. My next question to this witness will, of course, be whether this document is in relation to these principles of resubordination and attachment, whether that is in relation to the police as well. That's my next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the disciplinary aspect is concerned with whether when police are resubordinated to a military, the disciplinary infractions are carried out by the police chain of command or the military. It is not intended to suggest that military units resubordinated Anto units which were in fact like infantry units at that stage of the war in October, would not have had military disciplinary procedures carried out. Because obviously the TO was part of [indiscernible] -- was part of the military and it would be the military's job. Our argument is, as I've expressed very clearly, I believe, to the General, which he doesn't accept, is that police, when resubordinated, if at that stage they commit disciplinary offences, we say based on the evidence it is the police chain of command, and we therefore say this document does not assist one way or another. [Microphone not activated] No, Mr. Zecevic does not have a right in this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I didn't want to get up, but I just needed to. I must have -- must -- must stand up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER JUST SAID
utterances.text: "... we say based on the evidence it is the police chain of command, and we therefore say this document does not assist one way or the other." Clearly Ms. Korner is testifying now. She is making submissions. I -- I -- I go along with Mr. Krgovic, and I think that the document is relevant we do not object that it be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I take objection to this. It is not for Mr. Krgovic [sic] to stand up and -- this is not his witness. I should not have to deal with two different counsel, if not three. This is Mr. Krgovic's submission. We object, and I'm not giving evidence. There is no mention whatsoever, as the General has said, of the police in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this is not the first time that you have -- that -- an intervention about Mr. Zecevic's involvement in this, and the -- the -- we have not responded up to this point for the obvious reason that, although, strictly speaking, this is Mr. Krgovic's witness, this is an general understanding that -- that he is a common witness to the Defence. That aside, in this instance, we are satisfied on the basis of your objection that this document does not assist and ought not to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, now that we're dealing with disciplinary responsibility, is it possible in the military in a unit which is under the command of a military officer to have two different organs, to have two different systems be in charge of disciplinary proceedings and initiating them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In case there is a violation of military discipline, a case of -- of military duty while the combat is on, is it possible for somebody else outside of the military chain of command to investigate such cases and take steps in -- in connection with them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, during cross-examination, a number of questions were put to you with respect to co-ordinated action, and you explained that in your report. You explain how you viewed the co-ordinated action. And I will now show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show the witness P00680, tab 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that co-ordinated action between the MUP units and the army units did not automatically amount to resubordination. So would you please look at page 3 of this document. Paragraph 3.5 which is page 5 in the Serbian version. It says here: "When carrying out combat operations, the CSB and SJB units shall be under the direct command of the unit officers," and you explain that, "in keeping with the combat rules of the armed forces of Republika Srpska. In the event of co-ordinated action with the Army of Republika Srpska, the units shall be resubordinated to the command of the armed forces in charge of combat operations." General, the last page of this document is signed by chief of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin. Can you tell us, General, or, rather, can you give us your comments concerning this paragraph about the co-ordinated action between the police forces and the army.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, in my report, and also in my replies, I clearly and in detail explained that the notion of co-ordinated action not only in the former JNA and in the Army of Republika Srpska but in all armies is a strictly military notion which includes military forces, armed forces. Co-ordinated action cannot be carried out with somebody who has merely a work obligation. This is why the commander is first needed to give an appropriate status to a policeman who has a work obligation. He needed to be transferred into military obligation, and only then was it possible to have a co-ordinated action with this person who, thus, becomes a conscript. In accordance with the rules of international laws of war, one may kill members of armed forces. By giving the status of that person and making that person a military conscript, you automatically provide that person all the protection under the law and all the protection against any adverse consequences. This is why I emphasise that the term -- the notion of "co-ordinated action" is a strictly military term, unlike co-operation, which is a somewhat different notion. As for co-ordinated action, it always pre-supposes resubordination. It pre-supposes singleness of command and subordination. Yesterday, I did not have time to fully conclude this topic. Co-ordinated action could be of an internal nature, within that unit, and of an external nature. It can be between that unit and some other forces. However, in that case, the relations, the place, and the role of each individual is strictly defined, and one is always subordinated to one's commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mr. Zupljanin, in this document, says: "In case of co-ordinated action with the units of Army of Republika Srpska, units shall be resubordinated to the command of armed forces in charge of combat operations." Is this a correct attitude, a correct view?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only possible one. This is the only way in which one can protect the people involved in this, by defining it in this way. Otherwise, they would not be considered members of armed forces and they would not be permitted to take part in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, further on, it was suggested to you that resubordination of the police to the army in such large-scale operations, such as Operation Corridor, and that there were no such cases in practice. And I will show you some exhibits demonstrating this, P1298 or, rather, 1928. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To be accurate, I didn't put that there were no such cases in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this is a report on the work of the public security station in Donji Vakuf between the 1st of April, 1992 and 25th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 25th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So would you please look at the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The penultimate paragraph. The next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it begins with the following words: "In the middle of May, both active and reserve police forces actively joined the army in combat operations and in crushing the resistance in villages inhabited by Muslims." And then this paragraph goes on to describe these activities, and what I'm interested in is the last paragraph: "During participation in combat operations, the workers of the public security station were resubordinated to the command of the RS Army (the 19th Krajina Brigade)." Then they go on to give a number of 11 combat operations involving the police. General, would you please give a brief comment of this. Of the paragraph and of the report.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, this is yet another example which shows that it was only possible to use the police in combat operations via this mechanism by resubordination. By doing that, the status of policemen was changed, from one status to a different status. It is well known that it is only based on that status that, after the war, people can get various benefits, entitlements, compensation in case of injury, death, and similar consequences that can ensue in war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, during your testimony here, did either side show you a single document that would point to something completely opposite from what you described to us here, concerning the resubordination of police forces to the military in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll rephrase because I'm not quite precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a shown a single document that would make you change your conclusion about the principle of resubordination, as described in your report, and as explained here before the Trial Chamber during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krgovic. Not as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, would you please look at paragraph 133 of your report. Here, you deal with the issue of responsibility for the acts of the subordinates. It goes on to say: "A military officer is personally responsible for violations of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that a person subordinated to him or other units or individuals were preparing such violations."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe I asked a single question about that paragraph or on that issue at all in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll deal well that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm sorry. Before you can re-examine it has to arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be patient, Miss. Wait up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You quote footnote 60, the control and command, manual for military academies. The application of international law of war and the armed forces of the SFRY. That's in the footnote. General, what about a brigade commander who would have heard about this during his training, would that commander not have to be familiar with these regulations?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One, that's leading, and it's still not a matter that's come out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned the person of the brigade commander and his responsibility for subordination. I'm not mentioning the name for obvious reasons. You even quote something he wrote about his own responsibility for punishing subordinates. That stems directly from your cross-examination. You even specified a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Your Honours, I don't follow this at all, I'm afraid. What I quoted to the General and he declined to accept, as Mr. Krgovic rightly points out, and for the sake -- safety's sake, we better go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you appreciate the distinction? Ms. Korner's last comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, yesterday Ms. Korner showed you this paragraph about a specific situation. Or, rather, stated her position regarding this specific situation. My question: We have a resubordinated police officer, in a specific case, and a brigade commander, who was in charge of initiating disciplinary proceedings and who is authorised to take measures?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, as I've pointed out on more than one occasion, if a police officer is subordinated to a military unit commander, he is effectively a military conscript and has that status. In that case, it is the commander of the military unit that is responsible for initiating any proceedings or, indeed, pressing charges against this subordinated individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, General, do we take it to mean that this also includes disciplinary proceedings? In contrasts of criminal proceedings arising out of a -- a major offence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's right. Any kind of responsibility, moral responsibility, material responsibility, disciplinary responsibility, criminal responsibility. Your Honour, the status of that person in that case is the same of that of any other member of the unit for the duration of the resubordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, it strikes me as if we have come as far as we can possibly get with this witness in relation to the issue of proceedings -- okay. So I suggest that, again, in light of the time pressure that we are under this afternoon, that you move onto something else. Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am done with this. This was my last question on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, two days ago, you spoke about the concept of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness please be shown 65 ter 20259; tab 110, OTP. Could we please zoom in on the portion where it talks about combat. This is midway down the middle paragraph, or column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you quoted the military lexicon, describing combat as the basic and most widespread form of combat activity. General, what would be the broader concept here? Combat activity or combat?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, combat activities are the broader concept of the two. As is obvious, combat is one and perhaps the simplest form of combat activities. There are higher forms and more complex forms of combat activity, such as battle and operation, as the most evolved, most complex form that a combat activity may take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the conduct of an operation? Would that comprise a single action or several actions? And can you please explain.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, as I've said before, operation is the most complex form of combat activity. This means that it comprises a number of battles or situations of combat, the objective being to inflict as many losses on the enemy as possible throughout a war. In terms of character, in terms of substance, in terms of the number of men involved, it represents the most complex, the most evolved form of combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked a question about this. During the conduct of combat operations, while cleaning up, or mopping up, which category would that particular action belong to?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you're making me think back -- you make me remember all these details. In addition to combat and battle, as you suggest yourself, there are many other combat actions that are performed, as well as tactical actions or procedures. All of that might entail what you suggest; mopping up as a tactical action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is that part of combat activities?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That's right, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about combat task, a combat assignment?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, a combat task is clearly and precisely defined in relation to each unit, depending on its level, depending on the situation. One must define what that unit is expected to do specifically, within the framework of an operation, in a combat situation or in a battle. What it is expected to do in order to achieve the objective of a certain operation or the objective of certain combat activities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the question. The microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Performing a combat task, tactical operations, if I may put it that way -- or, rather, when we have a resubordinated unit, during these activities, were these resubordinated units under the command of the commander performing these activities?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll move onto a different subject now. General, during the resubordination process - and now the unit is subordinated to the military commander - so during the process itself, is the unit bound to carry out each and any of his orders during this situation, while all of this applies?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's right, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner asked you about POWs yesterday. What in case POWs are being transported, taken somewhere? What about securing the place where these POWs are assembled, put together? What about securing their transport to a camp?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the same thing applies. POW transport can be secured in a variety of ways. All of this is regulated by the military commander in charge, and he was put in charge by his superior commander. He must carry out this task. The commander in charge of transporting POWs is allowed to use certain units, certain equipment to make sure that the transport of POWs from point A to point B is safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you were asked yesterday whether you came across an order or a directive by the VRS invoking Article 104 of the Law on All People's Defence. General, what is the established practice in the army? When an order is issued, or when instructions are issued, does one usually invoke a particular article of the law, a particular rule, a particular provision?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krgovic. What applies in our case is do first and complain later. You receive an order, the preamble normally invokes in no uncertain terms another order by a superior officer, or one invokes a particular situation. It is based on that that you put together your own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you were shown a document yesterday. It's P2390.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness please be shown that document. The last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Situation in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Military District. "Propaganda activity and charges laid against the JNA as the main ... party ... responsibile for the recent events are continuing." General, you addressed this before this Honourable Tribunal. You talked about the effects of propaganda. Ms. Korner showed you this document during her cross-examination. Can you please tell us how this propaganda, if I may call it that, and documents such as these affected the way some components of the JNA treated those doing the actual propaganda?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I'm afraid I did not completely understand your question. My concentration may be wearing off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying not to put leading questions. In your report, you discuss this very issue of the attitude the JNA had vis-a-vis -- let me help you. When addressing propaganda aimed against the JNA. In this report, we see some propaganda activities aimed at the JNA. How did such activities impact the attitude of the JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, a similar method or scenario was used, starting from Slovenia, down to Bosnia, with the aim of breaking up the JNA. It was best achieved by people leaving its ranks. As I have said before, it started in Slovenia. Unusual situations began to take place, but one needs to expect that in a war. For example, in my own unit, there was an assistant commander of the battalion who abandoned his position, his position being a senior one, in order to join the Slovenian TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you seem to have gone off on a tangent. I'd like us to focus on the first part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at P2391 for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, let me ask you this: As the JNA was withdrawing, did its ethnic composition change, and, in what way, especially once you arrived Bosnia? What was the ethnic composition of the remaining part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I can only cite examples from my own unit, although I'm aware of similar situations elsewhere. I can say that most Slovenians and Croatians, including officers, as well as soldiers, remained behind. Many Muslims did stay with the JNA, as far as Bosnia, when they began leaving us. Macedonians and Montenegrins remained, as well as Albanian, Hungarians, and other ethnicities which were then represented in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have this report before us shown to you yesterday by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in. Item 2. The penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Part of the officers in the 92nd Motorised Brigade openly -- is openly against the JNA for not taking a different approach in Bijeljina and Zvornik, whereas, they do not apply the same standard when they refer to Bosanski Brod." Do you know which event they have in mind when they mention this ban on intervention?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, given the fact that this was in April, it could be the issue of the Posavina, although I'm not certain. It concerned an attack of the Croatian armed forces against the Serbs, or on the Serbs who lived there, although I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does Sijekovac ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to recall it, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show another document to the witness then, which is -- please bear with me. I seem to have written down an incorrect number. P20246. 65 ter 20246. Apologies. Tab 6A of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, it was suggested to you yesterday in relation to this document that the JNA did nothing. Please read carefully paragraph 4. The second sentence from the top: "However, in the morning hours, the activities became of higher intensity." "Party leaders do not control the situation and are not capable of stopping the activity. For this reason, they are unable to enforce the curfew between 8.00 p.m. and 6.00 a.m., and MUP, at present, refuses to participate in mixed patrols with the JNA." General, can you offer comments regarding this last sentence? What is the commander in question trying to say?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember that period, there were political negotiations round the clock, as well as different attempts to put a stop to these interethnic clashes. One such measure that was agreed upon was to conduct joint patrols, comprising members of the MUP and JNA. It seems that the arrangement, however, was not honoured and that it is that that is discussed in this part of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to your report. In footnote number 10, you mention a date. And you refer to a book: "Cessation Orchestrated by the Great Powers." General, did you use any part of this book or any of the positions put forth by its author in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us study the footnote for a moment. It is 35D2; 65 ter. Tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems I don't have the page I wanted to show, Your Honours. Perhaps we could take an earlier break by some five minutes so that I can come up with the appropriate page. And once we are back, I'll wrap up in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to ask your leave to more specifically define the position that I presented a while ago when I spoke about the status of members of the armed forces in relation to the provisions of the international law of war. I believe I was slightly imprecise when I said that a while ago. I have thought about it, and I think I'm getting a little tired, so that was probably the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. When I talked about resubordination as an act and the fact that they thereby become members of the armed forces, and under the rules of international law, it was allowed to kill them; and they thereby became legitimate targets. That is what I tried to say, and now I'm trying to be more precise about it and specifically define it. It is allowed to kill them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you've answered my question, but I'll move onto something else now. I showed you this book, Cessation Orchestrated by the Great Powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have OTP Exhibit 2235; tab 97. 2235. 20235. That's a 65 ter number. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you see the editors of this book and the reviewers. Professor Miodrag Starcevic is one of the names there. In answer to one of the questions by Ms. Korner, 23907, page 23907, specifically, you said -- 23965, you said that this was a book published by an institute with a good reputation and very good references. Do you know this gentleman, Miodrag Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, yes, I do know Professor Miodrag Starcevic. He is a well-known and well-regarded expert for international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at a document for me, just to make sure we mean the same person, we have the same person in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. 2D101233. The last page of the document, please. This is tab 118; Defence tab 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here, have a look. Miodrag Starcevic. His CV. A member of the international humanitarian fact-finding commission.
