utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I think I only met this gentleman once, so -- and even that was a long time ago. I was still working as head of the morale administration and as assistant chief of the General Staff. So this may be the same person I met back then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can we please go back to the Law on All People's Defence. Paragraphs 24 through to 26 are the ones we will be discussing. In the meantime, we have received a document from the OTP and I'll ask you to comment. It's in relation to that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 20264. OTP document 20264. Page 2, please. Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Work obligation units shall be organised for the needs of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ... in war and in the case of an imminent threat of war. Work obligation units shall be organised by assigning them to -- by assigning to them citizens subject to work obligation and not assigned to the armed forces or subject to work obligation in bodies of the Interior Ministry." General, to go back to your interpretation of this article, number 4, 25, 26, what about the provisions of this decree? Have a close look, please. Are they any different from the letter of the law; and are the two interpretations different?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, also, I think the General ought to be asked if he has ever seen it before in fairness to him, or if this is the first time he's seen this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner, I've come across this document already. I never had a chance to use it in my work though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer the question, General.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I'm looking at Article 1. I'm looking for a discrepancy. Then there is something there that confuses me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But my question was: Are there any discrepancies. If you don't see any, please state so.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this: "For the needs of the armed forces in war and in case of an imminent threat of war." I see that this classification was added in relation to what Article 26 says. It only says "in war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what about how it relates to Article 25?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I established a link between Article 25 and Article 26. In my opinion, the two are related. It reads: "Among other things, that those liable for work obligation must remain on their jobs and assignments, the ones they are performing, unless they are called to serve in the armed forces or assigned to other tasks and jobs." Specifically in relation to practical matters, the next paragraph says that such individuals may be assigned within their own place of residence or outside their place of residence. They must act in compliance with the assignment received. And then Article 26. It specifies who is responsible and who is authorised to change their war assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm really sorry. I would invite Mr. Krgovic or Your Honours to ask, and I'm sorry this arrived so late, but the simple question is this: Whether Article 1 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. The simple question is whether Article 1 of this particular regulation, if it's correct as published in the gazette, means that people who are assigned to work obligation for the minister [sic] of interior may not be assigned to the military. That's the -- the simple question. Do you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you have heard the question. Could you please answer it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not my interpretation. My interpretation is what the law says, the law that I used for my report, Ms. Korner. I see it as being very specific and clear. Workers assigned a particular work obligation during a war or during an imminent threat of war may change their war assignment, and, if called upon by the relevant bodies, they may also perform military duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while Mr. Krgovic is looking for his next document, can I say we're going to look for the official version and then, by agreement, we'll add it to the law library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I have a series of questions for you about the differences between the expert report that you produced for the Popovic case and the present one. You referred several times to the fact that these are two different reports. Can you please explain what that difference is reflected in? How are the two different? What does the difference comprise?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, in the briefest possible terms, the substantial difference between the two reports is the fact that we're dealing with two different cases. We are studying two different cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are we looking at the same time-period, the same time-frame? Both cases are two different ones. If so, each -- if so, which?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the focus of my second report, the present one, is on 1992; whereas, the first report did not have a limited time-frame. It was more about explaining the place and role of assistant commander for morale. Firstly, in general terms; and, secondly, in a war time situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, Ms. Korner spent quite some time in her cross-examination probing the introductory part of your report. Would you please open page 2 of your report and look at paragraph 2 and 3. General, it says here: "Introduction." And then please look at paragraph 14 where it says: "General Framework." Tell me, please, General, when you wrote this, the introduction and the general framework, what was your intention? What significance do you think this part of your report holds? Why did you use that methodological approach?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, in order to research the topic that I did, I had to place it in some general context which is described in the first part. And I also had to give it some temporal context, which is discussed in paragraph 14. I had to start from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the main focus, the main topic of your report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krgovic. As I have said throughout my report, when dealing with a command, organisation, rules and regulations, I attempted to deal with the very important topic that I put before myself because I considered that those cases or those phenomena of the use of police units and their resubordination to military commanders were possible or could be explained only by studying military rules and regulations because a war is waged in accordance with military rules and regulations and it is waged by soldiers, not by policemen. This is why I analysed the organisation, command, principles, and structure in order to confirm this position of mine which I considered to be the only possible [as interpreted] in these cases, in order - I emphasise - to classify or categorise those individuals as members of armed forces who would fall under the provisions of the international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, on page 23907, it was suggested to you by the Prosecutor -- or, rather, the previous page, 906 and 907, it was suggested to you that your idea was to ensure that the Defence got General Gvero acquitted for Srebrenica, that that was your goal when writing that report. And your reply was: "When I said that I wanted to assist the Defence, I wish to explain that my aim was to explain the principles existing in the army, and to assist, first and foremost, the Trial Chamber."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He said -- well, I'm sorry. [Microphone not activated] answer. He said, "You're right," to my question, and then added that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But not when you say that only helped General Gvero. "I wanted to explain this as a principle present in the army, and I wanted to assist the Trial Chamber, first and foremost ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, it was suggested to you by Ms. Korner, and on page 23872, she said to you that, as a Defence expert, you wanted to help the Defence. Could you explain to us what is your perception of the role of an expert in this case before this Court?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I understand that, as an expert before this Court, I have to be objective and unbiased. It is possible that prompted by the suggestion of Ms. Korner, I uttered those words. However, I emphasise and I have said earlier that I see my role, first and foremost, as that of an expert before this Trial Chamber. I see that my role is to help the Trial Chamber. Perhaps I was led in giving that answer by the position that I held for the longest time in my career. As you could see from my CV, I spent the longest part of my career in the position of an assistant, assisting sometimes the commanders to take difficult decisions. As you could see in my CV, at the end of my career, I held the position of a commander, and I had to then take difficult decisions myself, and I know that it's not easy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you drew conclusions and when you included them in your report, did anyone influence you, influence your conclusions and the views expressed in this report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you were not a Defence expert but an expert of the OTP or of any other side, would the views expressed in your report be different?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Krgovic, I claim with full responsibility that I would have provided identical answers, an identical report when it comes to this topic, resubordination to military -- of police to military commanders and military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: General, we are grateful for your willingness to assist the Tribunal, for your patience over the many days that you have been with us. And your persistence, despite your own personal difficulties. You would be pleased to know that you are now released, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. There are a few matters with which the Tribunal must deal before it rises, so I would ask the usher to escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And before that, can I say that whatever submissions I may be making about the General's evidence I too am grateful for his patience over what was, obviously, a very lengthy cross-examination and also his courtesy; although, I could have done without being called Ms. Korner every time he answered a question. But I am very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to thank you and this Trial Chamber for the understanding you have shown and for your fair treatment. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There are brief matters that the Chamber wishes to address, but before I do that, I don't know if counsel from either side have any observations or requests before we rise for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I imagine Mr. Krgovic wants to ask that Your Honours admit the report and the accompanying documents. As I've indicated to Mr. Krgovic and to Mr. Zecevic, I will be objecting to the admission of that report with some reasons for it, and I think we all feel that Monday morning would be better for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. The first matter is the admission of 659D1. In its decision of the 15th of September the Chamber marked for identification a document with Rule 65 ter number 659D1, pending the provision of a complete translation. As one has now been provided, we order that this -- the MFI qualification on this be removed and the document be admitted and marked as a full exhibit. And we record our appreciation for the assistance of Defence counsel in noting the situation with regard to this document. The second matter is the completion of the Rule 66(B) disclosure. And we note that now that we have a revised batting order from the Zupljanin Defence, we anticipate that the Prosecution can also confirm to the Chamber that its disclosure of Rule 66(B) material to the Defence pursuant to our decision of the 19th of August is now complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that -- are you asking me, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I paused. You may wish to -- when I say "you," the OTP may wish to return to this when we reconvene on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I do say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But I pause in the even that you are in a position to respond now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am, with the exception of one witness, who I think is still a query -- and I see Mr. Krgovic nodding, he is still a query even though he is still on the list. We have, otherwise, completed disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The final matter is estimates for cross-examination, and in order for forward planning and to make the most effective use of the limited time available, we invite both the Prosecution and the Stanisic Defence to provide the Chamber with its time estimates for cross-examination of all remaining witnesses no later than Thursday, next, that's the 22nd of September. And we take the opportunity to remind the Prosecution that with the exception of the three Rule 92 ter witnesses, it will be granted no more than the time estimated by the Zupljanin Defence for examination-in-chief. We also remind all parties of the requirements of guide-lines 25 to 27 of the procedural guide-lines on the presentation of evidence of Rule 92 ter witnesses. Estimates of time for cross-examination of the three Rule 92 ter witnesses were expected "as soon as possible" after the relevant decisions were issued on the 21st of July and the 22nd of August. And as we rise for the weekend, the Chamber wishes to acknowledge -- it would have earlier expressed its gratitude to CLSS for agreeing to accommodate the extended sitting today, and we wish to acknowledge the co-operation of everyone else who would have had to facilitate this. We -- especially the support staff, that is the security personnel, the court reporters, the court officers, and most of all, the accused, whose ordinary schedule would have been disrupted as a result of this extended sitting. So we thankfully have completed a little earlier than we thought we would have been here so -- You had something to add, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I just wanted to notify you that we made a submission for some documents to be added to our 65 ter list. This motion will reach you very soon. It has to do -- do with documents that we wanted to add to the list in relation to the next witness. The Prosecution has already been notified of this and I wanted to notify the Chamber as well, that we filed that motion, but it hasn't been distributed to the parties for technical reasons. Not yet. These are the documents that had been disclosed to us by the Prosecution. Some in August. And some earlier. All of these documents come from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we are alerted. Well, I trust that everyone has a safe weekend, and we reconvene, I think, Monday morning, and we're in the courtroom for the duration of this -- of the sitting of this case, during this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.12 p.m.,
